Cheng Li-wun became the first chairwoman of the Kuomintang (KMT) to meet Xi Jinping in a decade, prompting China to announce ten new measures and regular party-to-party channels, while Taiwan's president simultaneously hosted American lawmakers pressing for defence cooperation.

Ms Cheng called her Beijing trip a "peace mission" and told Mr Xi that if the KMT took power, she would invite him to visit Taiwan. She said the island should become "a symbol of peace jointly safeguarded by Chinese people on both sides of the strait." China announced ten new measures targeting Taiwan after the meeting, including resumed flights and regular communication channels between the KMT and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Even as Ms Cheng courted Beijing, Lai Ching-te, the president, met three American congressional delegations, saying that Taiwan's defence spending now exceeds 3% of GDP and will reach 5% by 2030.

Military pressure accompanied the diplomacy. Taiwan detected 17 Chinese aircraft and seven naval vessels on April 10th-11th, with 15 planes crossing the median line during the Cheng-Xi summit. The timing matched Beijing's habit of pairing talks with coercion.

Taiwan's economy continued its technology surge. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) reported record first-quarter revenue of NT$1.13 trillion ($35.6 billion), a 35% jump driven by AI chip demand from Apple and Nvidia. Mr Lai also opened the National Center for AI Robotics in Tainan, part of a NT$20 billion government investment from 2026 to 2029 to develop smart robots for medicine, services and high-risk jobs.

The opposition Taiwan People's Party expelled Li Zhenxiu, an at-large legislator, this week, stripping her of her seat. The move followed disputes over claims about Ann Kao, the mayor of Hsinchu, and questions about Ms Li's nationality and eligibility to serve.

Mark Carney's Liberal government is set to win a parliamentary majority this week, ending two years of minority rule through floor-crossings and by-elections that will reshape Canadian politics.

Marilyn Gladu became the fifth opposition MP to cross the floor to the Liberals, bringing the party to 171 seats — just one short of the 172 needed for a majority. Three by-elections on Monday are expected to deliver the rest. The shift would eliminate the Bloc Québécois's kingmaker role and give Mr Carney far more room to manoeuvre through his mandate, which runs to 2027 or 2028. An Ipsos poll shows 53% of Canadians want the Liberals to hold a majority.

The floor-crossings have triggered a crisis inside Pierre Poilievre's Conservative party. Up to 40 Conservative MPs reportedly fear losing their seats under his leadership, with some discussing invoking Reform Act provisions to force a leadership change. His communications director, Katy Merrifield, resigned this week. The turmoil sits uneasily alongside Mr Poilievre's 87% approval rating at the party's January convention, suggesting his MPs trust him far less than the party's members do.

In Quebec, members of the Coalition for Quebec's Future (CAQ) elected Christine Fréchette as their leader and the province's second female premier, replacing François Legault with 57.9% of the vote. She starts from behind: the Parti Québécois leads polls ahead of the October 2026 provincial election, which will complicate relations between Quebec City and Ottawa as the federal Liberals consolidate their majority.

Canada also moved to broaden its trade and defence ties. Mr Carney will meet Alexander Stubb, Finland's president, this week to strengthen cooperation on critical minerals, AI and quantum industries. The summit follows Mr Carney's March meeting with Nordic leaders.

The Bank of Canada held an emergency meeting with major lenders to discuss cybersecurity threats from Anthropic's Claude Mythos AI model, which can reportedly find vulnerabilities in operating systems and web browsers. Separately, Royal Bank of Canada announced a $1 billion growth fund to help Canadian companies grow at home rather than seek foreign capital, addressing weak productivity and reducing the pull of foreign markets.

Turkey's Kurdish peace talks have stalled because the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) has not disarmed, threatening Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's plan to change the constitution and extend his rule.

The PKK has cleared only seven of roughly 30 weapons caches along the Turkey-Iraq border, according to government sources. Turkey's intelligence service has not confirmed that the group has abandoned its arms despite formally announcing its dissolution. Without verified disarmament, the government cannot push through the constitutional changes it needs. Those changes require support from the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), which will not back them while the peace process remains incomplete. Abdullah Öcalan has sent new messages from prison urging the PKK to speed up, but the weapons remain.

Mr Erdoğan made clear this week that he will not call early elections, rejecting opposition calls for a snap poll. His government arrested Ümit Erkol, the Republican People's Party (CHP) chairman in Ankara, as part of a corruption investigation that the opposition called politically motivated. The party summoned all its provincial leaders to Ankara for an emergency meeting. The arrest fits a pattern of legal pressure on the opposition ahead of the 2028 election.

Turkey's confrontation with Israel escalated when Benjamin Netanyahu and his defence minister called Mr Erdoğan a "paper tiger" and tagged Turkish opposition figures on social media. The attacks prompted rare unity across Turkey's political spectrum, with opposition mayors and party leaders rallying to defend Turkish sovereignty despite their hostility to the president. Turkey also denied social media claims that Mr Erdoğan had said any attack on Iran or Lebanon would be treated as an attack on Turkey.

Turkey's central bank posted a record loss of 1.065 trillion lira for 2025. The loss reflects the cost of currency defence operations and the unorthodox monetary policies pursued between 2019 and 2023, when Mr Erdoğan fired multiple central bank governors for raising interest rates. Turkey's central bank posted a record loss of 1.065 trillion lira in 2025. The loss reflects the cost of currency defence operations and the unorthodox monetary policies Mr Erdoğan pursued between 2019 and 2023, when he fired multiple central bank governors for raising interest rates.
